passages.title: What is switched on today
passages.text: Built but not switched on yet on truehound.io: email sign-in links, alerts by email, the Slack app (reviews and requests inside Slack), the Microsoft Teams bot, Google sign-in, Microsoft Entra sign-in, connecting AWS IAM.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.text:
Truehound is an AI access agent. It finds who has access to your apps, removes what should be gone, and proves each removal by reading the app again. Start by looking at your own GitHub organization for nothing, or open the demo, then connect your apps and run one review.

What you need, and what is not on yet. The free scan and the live demo need no account. Everything else needs a Truehound workspace on a plan. Email sign-in links are not switched on yet: you sign in by payment, an activation code, an invite link or a passkey.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.heading: Try it before you buy
passages.text:
There are two ways in that ask for nothing. Neither one needs an account.
- The free scan reads your GitHub organization with a token you create. It shows the real score and counts, with names hidden, and finds former staff, outside admins, old deploy keys, public repos and secrets in code.
- The live demo is the whole product on a made-up company. Nothing you do in it touches a real app. There are also click-through tours, one per task.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.heading: Set up in this order
passages.text:
1. Open a workspace
 Pick a plan on the pricing page. The price is flat and never per seat. After you pay, the page Stripe returns you to signs you in. A teammate joins by an invite link from an admin. Later, a passkey saved on your device signs you back in. 2. Connect your identity source and your HR system
 Connect the system that says who is a current employee first. Truehound takes the leaving date from your HR system when you have one, and uses your identity provider to confirm it. If a person is suspended in the identity provider but still active in other apps, that is a finding. See Connect your apps for each way an app can be connected. 3. Connect the apps that hold your data
 Add your code host, cloud accounts and the apps your team uses. Each app has a card on the Sources page that says what Truehound can read, whether it can remove people through that app's own API, and which plan the vendor needs for that. 4. Read the people list and the Left, still has access board
 People shows one row per person across every app, with each account, role and last sign-in. Accounts that match no person are listed under No person for you to resolve. The Left, still has access board lists everyone who has left and still holds an active account somewhere, worst first, with a clock from the day they left. 5. Run your first review and keep the proof
 Start an access review, decide every line, sign off, and download the evidence pack.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.heading: Set up in this order
passages.text: Each change is sealed in Proof, a hash chain you can verify yourself.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.heading: Where things live
passages.text:
- Sources: connect, reconnect and check each app.
- People and Left, still has access: who holds what, and who should not.
- Access review and Review campaigns: run, schedule and sign off reviews.
- Access requests and Joiners and leavers: self-serve access, and the offboarding runs.
- Autopilot: the AI jobs and their switches.
- AI keys and agents: the AI keys and agents people created, and MCP hooks.
- Proof: every action, verifiable.
- Settings: your Anthropic key, roles, approvals and the developer tools.

passages.title: Getting started
passages.heading: What Truehound will not do
passages.text:
- It never calls someone departed unless you list them or your HR system or identity provider says so.
- It never shows a check it could not run as a pass. Apps it could not read are listed as not checked, with the reason.
- It counts a removal as done only when it has read the app again and the access is gone. A removal you did by hand is labelled manual and is not counted as verified.

---

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.text:
Every app on Sources is connected one of six ways. The card for an app tells you which, what Truehound reads from it, whether it can remove a person through the app's own API, and what plan the vendor requires for that. The integrations directory has a page for each app.

What you need, and what is not on yet. Which apps you can connect is listed on the integrations page, which counts only apps that are tested and switched on in the live build. Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID sign-in need Google and Microsoft client IDs that are not set up yet, and their cards say so. AWS needs Truehound's own AWS account on the connector, and its card says it is not set up on our side yet.

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.heading: The six ways to connect
passages.text:
- API token: you create a read-only token in the app (the card links to the right page and lists the steps) and paste it. Some apps need several values, such as a client ID and secret, and the card has one field for each.
- Browser sign-in (OAuth): you sign in to Google or Microsoft in your browser and grant read access. No secret is pasted, and the token is short-lived.
- SCIM: for apps that expose a SCIM user list on a plan that includes it, you paste the SCIM bearer token. Truehound reads the users and can deactivate them.
- Browser playbook: for apps with no user API on your plan, an admin stores a dedicated service account's sign-in. A scripted browser reads or removes members, limited to the app's own hosts. A page that has changed stops the run instead of guessing.
- Imported list: for an app with no API at all, you paste its users table, import its CSV, or read it from a screenshot or PDF. The import is the scan, and its file hash is sealed in Proof.
- Custom connector: for your own or niche app, you describe its users endpoint, authentication, paging and field mapping with no code, and it runs on the same engine as the built-in apps.

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.heading: Connect an app with a token
passages.text:
1. Open the app's card on Sources
 Search by name. The card lists what Truehound reads and the plan the vendor needs.

2. Create the token where the card points you
 Use the narrowest scope that reads users. Give a token that can remove people only if you want one-click removal, and only for apps where the card says removal is supported.

3. Paste it and connect
 Truehound reads the app once and shows what it found. If the vendor refuses part of the read, that part shows as not checked with the vendor's reason, and is never shown as a pass.

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.heading: What each card tells you
passages.text:
- Capability labels: read users, roles, last sign-in, revoke, verify, and which of those need a higher plan at the vendor.
- Whether removal works through the API. Some plans have no removal API at all, and the card says so once.
- Freshness. A review will not start on data that is stale. Imported lists stay fresh for 7 days.
- Plain error words. A refused token says what the vendor said and how to fix it.

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.heading: Identity and HR systems
passages.text:
Connect your identity provider (Okta, JumpCloud, Google Workspace or Microsoft Entra ID) and your HR system (for example BambooHR, Rippling, Deel, HiBob, Personio, Gusto, Workday or Kombo). The HR system is the authority on the day a person left. The identity provider corroborates it, and the page shows both dates and the gap when they differ.

Device managers (Jamf Pro, Kandji and Microsoft Intune) tie computers to people and appear on leavers' offboarding. They add devices, not accounts.

passages.title: Connect your apps
passages.heading: Where your credentials go
passages.text:
Without an account, tokens stay in your browser. With a team workspace, credentials an admin chooses to store for scheduled reads are encrypted on the server and never returned. See Security and data handling for how.

> Apps that need the connector's relay (because the vendor does not answer browsers) forward your token for that request only. The relay does not log it.

---

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.text:
An access review asks the right people to keep or remove each account in each app, records why, removes what they decide to remove, checks that it is gone, and gives your auditor a pack they can verify. Truehound builds the list, suggests a decision with a reason on every line, and refuses to sign off while anything is open.

What you need, and what is not on yet. Reviews, sign-off and the evidence pack work in a workspace and in the live demo. Recurring schedules that launch on the server need a team workspace. Delivery of reviews inside Slack and Microsoft Teams is built but not switched on yet, because the Slack app and the Teams bot are not registered. Reviewers outside Truehound get a link instead.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: Start a review
passages.text:
1. Check the scope
 Before launch you see the population: how many accounts across how many apps, how many are flagged, and who the reviewers will be.
 A freshness gate blocks the launch if an app's data is stale, so a review never freezes old data. Apps that could not be read are listed as not checked.

2. Launch
 Launching freezes a snapshot. Later changes in the apps do not move the lines under a reviewer.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: Decide every line
passages.text:
- Each line shows the person, the account, the role, last activity and the source, and the usage band where the app reports one.
- Each line carries a suggested decision with a one-line reason. Without an Anthropic key the suggestion comes from rules and is labelled as rules. With your own key, Claude can write the reasons, and that is an explicit per-workspace opt-in. See AI keys.
- A reason is required on every decision, keep or revoke. You can keep many lines at once with one comment.
- A reviewer cannot decide their own account. Reviewers can delegate a line with a reason, and an admin can reassign lines in bulk.
- A review can have one to three stages: a manager, an app owner, or named people. Stage two sees stage one's decision and reason.
- Accept a risk with a reason of 20 or more characters, a named owner and an expiry within a year. When it expires the line reopens by itself.
- Usage shown beside each line helps you justify a keep or a revoke.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: Revoke, then verify
passages.text:
A revoke decision removes the access through the app's API under your approval policy, then Truehound reads the app again. The line counts as done only when the re-read agrees. A cancelled dialog records nothing.

If the re-read still sees the account, or could not run, sign-off stays blocked until you try again, remove it by hand, or accept the risk with a written reason.

A removal done by hand carries a note and up to three screenshots or PDFs and a ticket link. They go into the evidence pack unchanged with their hashes. It stays labelled manual and is not counted as verified until a later read shows the account gone.

For privileged access, Truehound can remove every path to it, whether direct, through a group or through a role, and catch access that is inherited. It previews the effect first.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: Sign off
passages.text: Sign-off is named and carries an attestation. It is refused while any line or revoke is open. Reminders and escalation to the campaign owner are built, but they go out by email, which is not switched on yet.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: Schedule reviews
passages.text:
On Review campaigns, a signed-in workspace saves a recurring review on the server: monthly through annual, or every 1 to 365 days, full or delta (only accounts that are new, or whose roles or admin status changed, since the last run).

The server cron launches each schedule on its date with nobody in the app, once per date. It waits, and says why, while another review is open or no app has been read yet. A schedule can end on its due date and skip or revoke undecided lines, with each revoke going through the approval policy. You can also manage schedules as code with Terraform or the API.

passages.title: Access reviews
passages.heading: The evidence pack
passages.text:
- A ZIP with a CSV per system, the decisions with reasons, the revocations with their verification state, accepted risks, and escalations.
- A manifest with SHA-256 hashes of every file, so an auditor can check that nothing changed, and a PDF summary.
- A read-only auditor link to one pack, valid 1 to 90 days and revocable. Every view, download and check is logged for you.
- Control mapping to frameworks, and evidence expiry warnings before evidence goes stale.
- Automatic push of the pack to Vanta or Drata when you sign off, once you connect either on the Controls page.
- Every launch, decision, delegation, accepted risk and sign-off is sealed in Proof, which you can verify in the app, in the auditor's browser, or offline with the verifier included in the pack.

> Truehound does not hold a SOC 2 report or any certification. The pack gives your auditor the evidence of your own review.

---

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.text:
Offboarding in Truehound is one checklist for one person across every connected app. It removes access where an app's API allows, tells you exactly what you must do by hand for the rest, lists the apps it could not check, and ends with a receipt.

What you need, and what is not on yet. The Left, still has access board and the offboarding checklist work in a workspace and in the demo. Automatic removal when a leaver's run is approved is off by default and an admin switches it on, and it needs a team workspace. Hand-over of repositories and Drive files is built and needs a team workspace. An HR event opening a run on its own needs your HR system to send the event.

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.heading: Find who left
passages.text:
The Left, still has access board lists everyone suspended or deleted in your identity source, or marked as leaving in your HR system, who still holds an active account somewhere. A contractor past their end date counts too. The clock runs from the day they left to the last removal, and the worst case is first.

The leaving date comes from your HR system when you have one, then from your identity provider, so the board and the offboarding page always tell the same story. In the GitHub audit you can also paste the names of people who left, or upload a CSV, and every member and outside collaborator is checked against it.

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.heading: Run the offboarding
passages.text:
1. We can remove
 Apps where the connection allows removal. One click removes the person, then Truehound reads the app again to prove it held. You can remove every API account in one confirmation.

2. You remove, we check
 Apps with no removal API on your plan. The page gives you the admin link and the vendor's steps, you remove the person, and you mark it done. It is labelled manual and is not counted as verified until a later read shows the account gone.

3. Not checked
 Apps Truehound could not read are listed with the reason. They are never hidden and never shown as clean.

4. Finish and keep the receipt
 The receipt shows apps covered, how many removals were verified and how many were manual, and the time from the day they left. It is sealed in Proof and can be downloaded. A finished run stays as its receipt and is never planned again from scratch.

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.heading: Removal on approval
passages.text:
A leaver's run can remove the person through each app's own API when it is approved. An admin switches this on, it is off by default, and the switch is sealed in Proof. The approval shows how many apps it will remove the person from. Removal is verified by a re-read in the same way as in a review. The supported apps each cite the vendor's own documentation for the removal call.

Offboarding playbooks branch by exit type (voluntary, involuntary, contractor), department, title, location and app, with timed steps.

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.heading: Start a run from your HR system
passages.text: An HR termination sent to Truehound by webhook, or an identity provider's SCIM deactivation, opens the person's offboarding run at once. Admins are told, and the run waits for an approval. There is one run per person, and the trigger can be switched off per workspace. You can also start one through the API with a people event or an offboarding request.

passages.title: Offboarding
passages.heading: What else is covered
passages.text:
- Devices from Jamf Pro, Kandji and Intune appear on the leaver's page.
- Accounts that belong to no person are shown under No person, with suggestions you can accept, dismiss or snooze, so a leaver's second account is not missed.
- The reasons and the elapsed time feed the leaver reconciliation in the evidence pack, as hours from leaving to removal.

> Slack below the Business+ plan has no removal API. Truehound says so on the card and gives you the manual steps.

---

passages.title: Access requests
passages.text:
An access request is a short form: which app, which role, why, and for how long. The right person approves or denies with a reason. Truehound grants the access through the app and checks it, or hands the work to the app's owner as a task. Every step is recorded in Proof.

What you need, and what is not on yet. Access requests need a team workspace and, for each app, a connection that can grant access. Requests and approvals inside Slack and Microsoft Teams are built but not switched on yet, because the Slack app and the Teams bot are not registered. Email approvals need email sending, which is not on yet. Approving in Truehound works today.

passages.title: Access requests
passages.heading: Make an app requestable
passages.text:
On the Access requests page an admin picks which connected apps people may request, which roles, and who approves: the owner, the manager, or the manager and then the owner. The approval policy sets how many people approve, and an admin role needs more.

An app with no owner says so in plain words, and the request goes to an admin.

passages.title: Access requests
passages.heading: Request, approve, grant
passages.text:
1. The employee asks
 They choose the app and role, say why, and say for how long. The request shows the seat cost, any unused seats that could be reused instead, and the department's budget impact.

2. The approver decides
 An approver approves or denies in Truehound or through the API. Once the Slack app is registered, they can do it in Slack too. A denial must carry a reason, and the requester sees it. Separation-of-duties rules are enforced at request time.

3. Truehound grants and checks
 It grants the access through the app's API, SCIM, or the identity provider's groups, then reads the app again before calling it granted. If the app has no API, the request becomes a task for the owner with evidence.

4. Time-bound access ends on time
 Access with an end date counts down. At expiry, the server removes it, restores the role the person had before, and reads the app again. The requester can end it early.

passages.title: Access requests
passages.heading: More ways in
passages.text:
- The employee App hub lists apps people can request and shows their own access and who administers each app.
- Claude, through the MCP server, and the API can list, request, approve, deny and cancel requests as the person whose token is used, under the same approval policy and with the same rule that nobody approves their own request.
- Tasks for an app's owner can be pushed as tickets to Jira or ServiceNow, with field mapping and the ticket kept as evidence.
- When an app has no seats left, the request offers reclaiming an unused one or buying another.

passages.title: Access requests
passages.heading: Let Autopilot handle the routine ones
passages.text:
The Autopilot grant job can approve routine requests inside rules you set, for a set time, and send unusual ones to a person with its reasons. See Autopilot.

---

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.text:
Autopilot is the AI that does the routine access work, within limits you set and cannot be talked out of. Each of its five jobs is off, prepare for approval, or act alone. Whatever it does is in a log in the first person with its reason, and a change counts as made only when a re-read of the app confirms it.

What you need, and what is not on yet. Autopilot runs on the team server, so it needs a team workspace, and it is off until an admin switches it on. It works on rules alone. Claude writes the reasons only when your workspace has added its own Anthropic key and opted in, and every action says which one decided. The live demo shows Autopilot over the demo's sample findings.

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.heading: The five jobs
passages.text:
- Triage new findings: gives every new finding a priority (now, today or this week) and the reason. Modes: off or auto. It starts on auto.
- Remove stale and risky access: removes dormant accounts (30 to 365 days without a sign-in, 90 by default), unexpected guests and the agent's detections, in the apps you name, then re-reads each app. At most 1 to 100 accounts per run, 10 by default.
- Grant routine requests: grants requests that fit the approval step's rules for a set time, proves it with a re-read, and removes the access when the time is up. Anything unusual goes to a person with the reasons.
- Pre-fill reviews and chase reviewers: fills every open review line with keep, revoke or a person should look, citing the facts. It chases reviewers who have not answered after 2 days by default and escalates after 5.
- Run leavers end to end: removes a leaver's accounts, re-reads each app, reclaims the seats and records the saving, and files the evidence.

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.heading: Off, approve or auto
passages.text: Approve means Autopilot prepares the change and a person approves it. Auto means it acts alone inside the job's rules. The remove, grant, review and leaver jobs start on approve. Nothing runs until an admin switches Autopilot on. A cron picks up every workspace that has it on and has not stopped it.

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.heading: Rules nobody can loosen
passages.text:
- Never an admin role. It never grants one, never pre-fills keep on one, and never removes an admin account alone.
- Never a two-approval policy. Where your approval policy asks for two or more approvals, people approve.
- Never a deny without a person. Autopilot escalates with reasons. Only a person denies a request.
- Everything it reads from apps, tickets and requests is data, never an instruction to it.
- The kill switch stops every job before its next action.

> A setting that would loosen one of these rules is refused by the server, whatever the value.

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.heading: The kill switch, the log and undo
passages.text:
- The kill switch is always in reach. It records who pressed it and why, and is checked before every action. Resume is an admin action.
- The live log has one row per action: what it did, in the first person, the reason, who decided (rules, or Claude on your own key, checked against the rules), and the evidence.
- An admin can undo an action where the app allows it. Every action is also one event in Proof.
- The page leads with what it did: changes made, how many a re-read confirmed, what waits for a person, and what was undone.

passages.title: Autopilot
passages.heading: How it uses Claude
passages.text:
Claude has no tools in Autopilot. Its answers are checked against the rules before anything acts. Without your own Anthropic key every job runs on rules and says so. See AI keys for how to add one and what is sent.

---

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.text:
Every AI feature in Truehound runs on your own Anthropic key. An admin pastes the key once, switches AI on, and the charges go to your own Anthropic account. If you never add a key, nothing is sent to Anthropic and everything works from rules.

What you need, and what is not on yet. AI is off by default. Truehound has no key of its own for customers, and pays nothing for your AI. Without your key every feature runs its rules and is labelled as rules. The key and the opt-in are per workspace and need a team workspace. Provider inventory of AI keys covers OpenAI, Anthropic and GitHub Copilot.

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.heading: Add your Anthropic key
passages.text:
1. Create a key in your Anthropic account
 Use a key made for Truehound so you can see its usage and revoke it on its own.

2. Paste it under Settings, AI
 Truehound proves the key works with one call that lists models, which costs nothing, then stores it encrypted (AES-256-GCM, under a key derived for your workspace). Only its last four characters are ever shown again.

3. Opt in
 A consent screen lists exactly what is sent to Anthropic. One switch turns AI on for every AI use in the workspace. You can turn it off again at any time.

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.heading: What it does to your data
passages.text:
- Only the facts a feature needs are sent: for review suggestions, each row's app, name, email, roles, status, last sign-in, and admin, two-step and guest flags. The consent screen lists the rest.
- The key is never in a response, a log, an export or an audit line. You can replace or remove it, and each change is sealed in Proof with who made it and the last four characters, never the key.
- Anthropic's commercial terms bar training on customer content (Anthropic commercial terms, Customer Content).
- A usage meter shows calls and tokens this month, taken from Anthropic's own responses. There is an hourly rate limit per workspace.

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.heading: What turns on
passages.text:
With a key and the opt-in: reasons on review lines, the review and approval step, request decisions inside your rules, guided fixes, the campaign builder, the assistant, scheduled agents, and Claude on Autopilot and in drafted MCP hook policies.

Without a key, each of those runs its rules, labelled as rules, and the app shows an empty state that tells you to add a key.

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.heading: AI keys and agents, the inventory
passages.text:
The AI keys and agents page is a different thing: it is the inventory of AI keys other people created. It reads every AI API key, project, service account and Copilot seat from the providers' admin APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic and GitHub Copilot), with its owner and its last use where the provider reports one.

A revoke there counts only when a fresh read agrees. Beside the keys it shows the AI agents and connections Truehound already sees: MCP servers and agent tokens, sign-ins to AI apps reported by the browser extension, AI bots in connected apps, and OAuth grants to AI apps from Google and Microsoft.

When a person leaves, the agents, tokens and apps they created can be offboarded with them. The live demo shows this page on a fictional company.

passages.title: AI keys (bring your own key)
passages.heading: AI spend
passages.text:
Spend by person, team and model, with budgets per workspace and team, a month-end forecast and spike alerts, is on the same page.

---

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.text:
Two separate things share the MCP name. An MCP hook runs in your developers' AI clients and asks Truehound allow, ask or deny before each tool call. The MCP server lets Claude and other assistants read your access data and file requests in Truehound, under the same approvals as a person.

What you need, and what is not on yet. Both need a team workspace. The hook is an open script that needs Node 18 or newer. Drafting hook policies with Claude needs your own Anthropic key, and without one the drafts come from rules. The endpoint is the address shown on your workspace's Developers page.

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.heading: MCP hooks: govern calls without a gateway
passages.text:
A small open script runs in the agent client before each tool call. It sends one small request to your workspace and turns the answer into the client's own hook output. Nothing is rerouted: the tool call still goes from the client straight to the MCP server. Read every line of the script before you install it.

Supported clients: Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code Copilot (preview) and Codex CLI, each through its own documented hook.

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.heading: Install the hook
passages.text:
1. Create a hook token
 On AI agents, MCP hooks, create a token for the workspace, or one per person so every call is tied to that person. It is shown once.

2. Run the install command on each laptop
 The page shows a command for your client that downloads the script and installs it. It reads the token from an environment variable, writes it to a file only the user can read, and adds the hook to the client's user config. Running it again updates it and never adds a second entry.
 For managed laptops, print the client config and deploy it by MDM instead.

Shape of the install command (the page fills in your token and address):

``
curl -fsSL https://truehound.io/hooks/truehound-hook.mjs -o /tmp/truehound-hook.mjs
TRUEHOUND_HOOK_TOKEN=<token> node /tmp/truehound-hook.mjs install --client claude-code --api <address>
``

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.heading: What the hook sends, and how it behaves
passages.text:
- A summary of the tool input, at most 2,000 characters, with secrets replaced by [REDACTED] on the laptop first. The server redacts again before it stores anything.
- The request is abandoned after 250 milliseconds. An allow is cached for the time your workspace sets (60 seconds by default), so a repeated call makes no request.
- If Truehound is unreachable, your workspace's fail mode decides. Open, the default, lets the call run and keeps a record to send next time. Closed denies it. A policy can set its own.
- The option for all tools also checks built-in tools such as shell commands. The browser option also checks the client's own web fetch and search, so an agent's browsing is governed by site.

> The hook cannot see a person driving a browser, or an agent that drives a browser with no tool call through the client. The Truehound browser extension does not observe agent browser actions.

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.heading: Policies and evidence
passages.text:
- Policies allow, ask or deny by MCP server, tool, user, group or an input pattern, with a monitor mode that records without blocking.
- Every MCP server seen is listed, approved or not (shadow MCP), and you approve one in a click.
- Policies can be drafted from your last 30 days of history, by Claude on your own key or by rules, with each rule's impact before you apply it.
- Every call is kept redacted for the retention you set (365 days by default), measured latency is shown, and the calls export as CSV.

passages.title: MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude
passages.heading: Truehound in Claude: the MCP server
passages.text:
Truehound serves a remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP, JSON-RPC) at the /mcp path of your API address. Anyone in the workspace can make a token for themselves. A token can be read only, and can expire after 1 to 365 days. Claude and other MCP clients can also sign in with OAuth 2.1, with a consent page, short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens that rotate. An admin sets token lifetimes and the client hosts that are allowed.

Tools include who_has_access, find_person, list_leavers, offboard_person, proposal_status, list_access_requests, approve_request, deny_request, cancel_request, review_status, decide_review_rows, start_review, list_unused_licenses, open_ticket and change_role. The Developers page lists every tool and whether it reads or files something.

Writes never change an app directly. A removal or role change files a proposal that people approve under your approval policy, a decision is made as the token's person under the same policy, and nobody can approve their own request. A reviewer decides only their own rows. Every call is sealed in Proof.

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.text:
Everything the app shows about people, accounts, findings, reviews, offboardings, evidence and Proof is available over a REST API, and so are the actions: requesting and approving access, launching and deciding reviews, and starting offboardings. Webhooks tell your systems when something changes.

What you need, and what is not on yet. The API, webhooks and SIEM streaming need a team workspace. The address to call is shown on your workspace's Developers page, because the api.truehound.io name is not live yet. The OpenAPI 3.1 file is served at /api/v1/openapi.json on that address, and the Developers page renders every operation from it.

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Make an API key
passages.text:
1. Open Developers in your workspace
 Choose the scopes the key needs, such as people:read or config:write.

2. Copy the key once
 A key belongs to one workspace. Truehound stores only its hash, so the key is shown a single time. It has the form th_ followed by an id and a secret.

3. Call the API
 Send the key as a Bearer token. A key without the scope an operation needs is refused with 403.

Read your people (use the address your workspace shows):

``
curl <your-api-address>/api/v1/people \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TRUEHOUND_API_KEY"
``

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Basics
passages.text:
- Lists answer { data, next_cursor }. Pass next_cursor back as cursor to get the next page.
- Errors answer { ok: false, error, message }, with the field or scope named in plain words.
- The limit is 600 requests a minute per key.
- Data is what your workspace last published from each app, so it matches what your team sees.
- The API covers people, accounts, systems, findings, leavers, reviews (launch, assign, decide, sign off), offboardings, lifecycle runs, access requests (create, approve, deny, cancel, remind, revoke), evidence, access-path queries, Proof events and verification, review schedules, role bundles, custom roles, the approval policy, separation-of-duties rules, webhooks and SIEM destinations.
- The whole reference, with request and response fields and a curl line for each operation, is on the Developers page.

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Webhooks
passages.text:
Truehound posts an event to your https endpoint when something changes, once per change. You make an endpoint in Developers or with the API, and its signing secret is shown once. You can rotate it, send a test event, read the delivery log, and send any delivery again.

Events: leaver.detected, review.launched, review.signed, review.ended, revoke.verified, revoke.failed, offboarding.started, offboarding.completed, finding.created, finding.resolved, source.connected, proof.sealed, access.requested, access.approved, access.denied, access.granted, access.revoked, lifecycle.run_planned, lifecycle.run_completed, person.changed and ping.

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Check the signature

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Stream Proof to your SIEM
passages.text: Proof can be streamed as OCSF to an S3 bucket, Splunk HEC, Datadog or a signed webhook, set up as SIEM destinations in Developers or over the API. Each destination has a test and a delivery log. The export of every admin action is also available as a file.

passages.title: API and webhooks
passages.heading: Also for developers
passages.text:
- Manage schedules, the approval policy, role bundles and webhooks as code with the Terraform provider.
- Let Claude and other assistants work with your workspace through the MCP server.
- Sign people in to Truehound with SAML 2.0 or OIDC on email domains you prove you own, with roles from your IdP groups, and provision them with SCIM.
- Add an app Truehound does not have with the no-code custom connector described in Connect your apps.

passages.title: Terraform provider
passages.text:
Review schedules, the approval policy, role bundles and webhooks are the parts of a Truehound workspace that belong in code review. The provider manages them through the public API, so a change to who approves a fix goes through a pull request like any other change.

What you need, and what is not on yet. The provider is not on the Terraform Registry yet, so you cannot install it with a plain terraform init today. It has been applied against the production API, and a second plan found no drift. For a build of the provider, email truehoundhq@truehound.io. It needs a team workspace and an API key.

passages.title: Terraform provider
passages.heading: What it manages
passages.text:
- truehound_review_schedule: a recurring access review, with cadence, systems, reviewers, due days, full or delta mode, and what happens at the due date.
- truehound_approval_policy: the one approval policy per workspace. Destroying it resets the default.
- truehound_role_bundle: a named set of system and role grants.
- truehound_webhook: a signed webhook endpoint. The signing secret is kept in state as a sensitive value.
- truehound_webhook_events (data source): every webhook event type.

passages.title: Terraform provider
passages.heading: Configure it
passages.text:
1. Make an API key
 In Developers, API keys, make a key with the config:read, config:write, webhooks:read and webhooks:write scopes. See API and webhooks.

2. Point the provider at your workspace
 Set TRUEHOUND_API_KEY, and TRUEHOUND_ENDPOINT to the API address your workspace shows. The provider defaults to api.truehound.io, which is not live yet.

A quarterly review as code:

``
resource "truehound_review_schedule" "quarterly" {
 name = "Quarterly SOC 2 access review"
 cadence = "quarterly"
 start_date = "2026-11-01"
 systems = ["slack", "okta", "github"]
 reviewer_mode = "named"
 reviewers = ["ana@example.com", "lee@example.com"]
 due_days = 14
}
``

passages.title: Terraform provider
passages.heading: Drift and import
passages.text:
Terraform reads each object back from the API, so a change made in the app shows as drift in the next plan. Existing schedules, roles and webhooks can be imported. A schedule that Terraform manages is launched by the same server cron as one made in the app.

Change history on every configuration object shows who changed it and when.

> The provider creates and deletes real objects and can reset the approval policy. Try it in a test workspace first.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.text:
SCIM is used in four different ways in Truehound. They are separate features, and you can use any one without the others.

What you need, and what is not on yet. SCIM needs a team workspace. Truehound's SCIM client covers a fixed set of apps (listed below), not every SCIM app, and the SCIM bridge is self-serve, not a managed service. Both take effect only with the apps' own plans that allow SCIM.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.heading: 1. Your identity provider provisions people into Truehound
passages.text:
Truehound is a SCIM 2.0 server (RFC 7643 and 7644). Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, JumpCloud or OneLogin push users to it, with the base path /api/scim/v2 on your API address and a bearer token that Setup shows once.

The provider's pushes drive the lifecycle. A new user runs your joiner steps, a new department or title runs the mover steps, and a deactivation puts the person on the Left, still has access board and opens their offboarding for approval. Users are created, replaced, patched and deleted, and groups are supported.

Pushed groups map to Truehound roles for Okta (Push Groups) and Entra (group assignment). A user gets the highest role mapped to one of their groups, otherwise the roles attribute, otherwise member. An owner is never changed. Every write is sealed in Proof.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.heading: 2. Truehound provisions and deactivates people in apps
passages.text:
Over SCIM, Truehound can create a user with a role or group, change the role, and deactivate the user, then read the app again to prove each change. The apps with SCIM provisioning built in are Figma, Slack, Atlassian, Notion and Zoom, and Miro, monday.com and Canva for removal.

Slack needs a plan that includes SCIM. Provisioning and removal run under your approval policy.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.heading: 3. Truehound reads an app through its SCIM endpoint
passages.text: For apps that expose SCIM on a plan that includes it, you paste the SCIM bearer token on the app's card. Truehound reads the user list and can deactivate users. Each app is tested against its documented responses. The integrations directory marks which apps connect this way.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.heading: 4. The SCIM bridge: SCIM for an app that has none
passages.text:
On the SCIM bridge page an admin makes a SCIM 2.0 endpoint for an app that has no SCIM. Behind it is the app's API, through a custom connector, or a browser playbook. It has its own bearer token, shown once, and its path is /api/scim-bridge/<id>/v2 on your API address.

Your identity provider then deprovisions people in that app like in any SCIM app. A deactivation uses the app's own call, then Truehound reads the app again. The identity provider gets success only when that read agrees.

Okta's PATCH, Entra's string booleans and DELETE all deactivate. Creating a user works only when you set a create call on a custom connector. Attribute changes other than deactivation, and groups, are not written to the app. Every call is listed and sealed in Proof without a body or credential.

passages.title: SCIM
passages.heading: SSO into Truehound is separate
passages.text:
Signing people in to Truehound uses SAML 2.0 or OIDC per workspace, on email domains you prove you own, and is set up under Developers. See API and webhooks.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.text:
Truehound reads people, accounts, roles, status, dates and grants from the apps you connect. It never reads message, document or email bodies. Without an account, what you connect stays in your browser. With a team workspace, the workspace is kept in Cloudflare D1 and every change is sealed in Proof.

What you need, and what is not on yet. This page summarizes the Trust Center, which is the full statement and lists what is in place, what is partly in place and what is not yet. Truehound has no SOC 2 report, does not hold ISO 27001 and has had no independent penetration test yet.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: What Truehound reads, and what it never reads
passages.text:
- From connected apps: people, accounts, roles, status, dates and grants.
- Never the content of messages, documents or emails. Mailbox discovery is limited to the sender, subject and date.
- Secret values found in code are masked and never kept.
- Apps it could not read are listed as not checked. They are never shown as clean.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: Where your data lives
passages.text:
Without an account, the token, the audit and the workspace are stored in your browser, not on our servers. The token goes to the vendor, and through our connector only for apps that do not answer browsers or for GitHub code search. The connector relays it per request and does not store or log it.

With a team workspace, the workspace lives in Cloudflare D1. The website is static files on GitHub Pages with no server code. The connector and account backend are a Cloudflare Worker. We run no servers of our own. Every account query is limited to the workspace it belongs to, and automated tests check that a non-member gets not found.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: How credentials are protected
passages.text:
- App credentials an admin chooses to store, including sign-ins for browser playbooks, are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived for each workspace from a master secret held only in the connector's secret store, and are bound to their workspace and app. The master key can be rotated. They are never returned to the browser.
- Sign-in links, sessions, invites, API keys and extension keys are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. An API key is shown once.
- Your Anthropic key is stored the same way and only its last four characters are ever shown. See AI keys.
- Truehound has no passwords. You sign in by payment, an activation code, an invite link or a passkey, and the session cookie is HttpOnly and Secure.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: Control over changes
passages.text:
- Owner, admin and member roles, with custom roles and per-area read, edit and act permissions, limit who can change what.
- An approval policy can require one or more approvals, including a second admin, before a fix runs. The person who proposed a fix can never approve it.
- Every change, approval and consent in a workspace is written to Proof, a SHA-256 hash chain where tampering shows. You can verify it in the app and offline, and stream it to your SIEM.
- Autopilot's fixed rules and kill switch limit what automation can do. See Autopilot.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: How long data is kept
passages.text:
An owner can export everything a workspace holds as one JSON file, and can delete the workspace and everything stored for it in one step. A person can delete their own account. A privacy request is answered within 30 days, and customers are told of a personal data breach within 72 hours.
- Sign-in links work for 15 minutes and their records are deleted after 24 hours. A session lasts 30 days from your last visit.
- Scan history is kept 90 days, and the latest successful scan is always kept. Connected-app scans follow the same rule.
- Review links for reviewers outside Truehound expire 120 days after they are made. Invites expire after 7 days.
- Browser-extension sign-in sightings are kept 395 days. Demo-form leads are kept 24 months.
- Restore copies of account data expire within 30 days.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: What we do not have yet
passages.text:
- No SOC 2 report, and no ISO 27001. We do not claim either and will not until an independent auditor issues one.
- No independent penetration test yet.
- Backups are automatic, but we have not yet practised a restore. There is no uptime commitment unless an order form gives one.
- One person, the founder, can reach production.

> The Trust Center has the plan for each gap. Security questionnaires are answered directly, usually within 5 business days, at truehoundhq@truehound.io.

passages.title: Security and data handling
passages.heading: Also published
passages.text:
- Sub-processors, with 30 days' notice before one is added or replaced.
- The Data Processing Agreement, Master Service Agreement and service levels under Legal.
- A responsible disclosure policy with safe harbour, acknowledgement within 1 business day, and fix targets of 14 days for critical and 30 days for high issues: security disclosure.
- The accessibility conformance report and the public status page.

passages.text: Does Truehound replace Vanta? No. Truehound does not run a compliance program, manage policies or work with your auditor. It finds access that should not exist, removes it with your approval, and hands you proof. Does Vanta remove access when a reviewer denies it? Not through the review: per its help center, denying a user starts a remediation flow. Its offboarding does remove accounts automatically in six apps (Calendly, Zoom, Figma, Dropbox, Duo and Tailscale, per its release notes as of the date below); for other apps it assigns tasks. Can I upload Truehound's evidence into Vanta? That is what the evidence pack is built for: one CSV per app plus a manifest, laid out the way auditors ask. It ships with the access review plans.

passages.heading: The short answer
passages.text: Choose Drata to automate SOC 2 and other frameworks end to end. Choose Truehound for the removing: Drata's help center says its access review is focused on review and does not include remediation. Truehound removes access with your approval and keeps the proof.

passages.title: Truehound vs Drata
passages.heading: Where Drata is stronger
passages.text: A full compliance automation platform across many frameworks, with continuous control monitoring and an auditor workflow. Typed warnings in the review (former personnel, missing MFA, unlinked users, service accounts, admins) that double as filters. Evidence attached automatically to the access review control, with a renewal date. Hundreds of integrations and a Jira automation for offboarding evidence.

passages.title: Truehound vs Drata
passages.heading: Where Truehound is different
passages.text: It removes access from the finding, under your approval policy, instead of leaving removal to you. The review starts from a frozen snapshot, so the evidence shows access as of the review date. Reviews are included in every review plan, not an add-on, and the price is public. Proof is a re-read of the app, not an uploaded file or a ticket link.

passages.title: Truehound vs Nudge Security
passages.heading: The short answer
passages.text: Choose Nudge if your biggest problem is not knowing which SaaS apps people signed up for. Choose Truehound if you know your apps and need leavers removed, with proof, on a monthly price. For apps outside single sign-on, Nudge asks the app's owner to remove the account; Truehound removes it through the app's API where one exists.

passages.text: Discovery: Nudge finds apps from signup emails, OAuth grants and a browser extension. Truehound does not read email and has no browser extension. A mature offboarding playbook that locks the person out of Google or Microsoft, transfers critical resources and revokes OAuth grants. A trial with no sales call and no payment details, which Truehound does not offer (we offer the free scan and the live demo instead). Flat pricing up to 150 users, with every feature in every tier.

passages.title: Truehound vs Nudge Security
passages.heading: Where Truehound is different
passages.text: It removes access through each app's API where one exists, instead of asking someone else to. It reads the app again after removing, so the proof is the app's own answer. Monthly billing, cancel in the product. Nudge's published plans are billed annually. GitHub depth: deploy keys, outside collaborators, webhooks, public repos and secrets in code.

passages.text: Choose AccessOwl if you want access requests, approvals and onboarding run inside Slack across hundreds of apps. Choose Truehound if you want a flat price, reviews that schedule themselves, and offboarding that starts when someone is suspended in Google or Entra.

Slack-native: approvals, reminders and tasks happen where the team already works. Completed reviews sync to Vanta automatically. More integrations today: AccessOwl lists more than 400. Truehound connects far fewer, and says which. Its trust center lists SOC 2. Truehound holds no SOC 2 report. Public pricing and a self-serve trial.

passages.heading: The short answer
passages.text: Choose Okta when you need enterprise single sign-on, adaptive MFA and automated provisioning across many apps, and have someone to run it. Choose Truehound when Google Workspace or Entra is already your directory, you are 10 to 200 people, and the job is catching leavers in every app, removing their access with approval, and proving it to an auditor, at a flat price instead of per seat.

passages.title: Truehound vs Okta
passages.heading: Where Okta is stronger
passages.text: Single sign-on and MFA for your whole company, with adaptive policies. Truehound offers neither. Automated provisioning and deprovisioning through Lifecycle Management for apps it is connected to. A very large prebuilt integration network and years of enterprise use. A dedicated identity team can do far more with it: device trust, complex group rules, many directories.

passages.title: Truehound vs Okta
passages.heading: Where Truehound is different

It looks at the access that never passes through a sign-in: GitHub outside collaborators, deploy keys, secrets in code. After a removal it reads the app again and keeps the result as evidence, labelled verified, manual or still present.

passages.title: Truehound vs C1
passages.heading: The short answer
passages.text: Choose C1 if you have a security or IAM team and need access requests, lifecycle, access reviews and identity security in one platform, with hundreds of integrations. Choose Truehound if you are small, want a flat public price you can pay by card, and mainly need leavers and stale access removed with proof.

passages.title: Truehound vs C1
passages.heading: Where C1 is stronger
passages.text: A whole identity platform: lifecycle, access requests, just-in-time access, access reviews, identity security and governance of agents. Recurring review campaigns with templates, auto start and end, scoping by risk level or compliance framework, and revoking inherited access through groups. A public API, a Terraform provider and an open-source connector SDK. SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001 and HIPAA listed on its trust center. Truehound holds none of these. A larger integration catalog: its site has hundreds of integration pages. Truehound connects far fewer apps.

After removing access it reads the app again and keeps the before and after. GitHub depth: outside collaborators, deploy keys, webhooks, public repos and secrets in code are their own findings.

passages.title: AI agent control
passages.heading: Two weeks of agent tool calls
passages.text: Sample workspace: Acme. Each call went through the hook's own redaction and the server's own rule check, in your browser, against Acme's three rules.

passages.title: AI agent control
passages.heading: What makes it work
passages.text: 01. An open hook you can read. The hook is one file with no dependencies. Read every line before you install it. It sends a short summary of each call to your workspace and turns the answer into the client's own hook output; nothing is rerouted. Read the hook script. 02. A check before every action. The client asks before each tool call. Your rules answer allow, ask or deny by server, tool, person, group, input pattern or website. The request gives up after 250 ms; a workspace or a rule decides whether a call that cannot be checked runs or stops. 03. Five AI clients. Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code Copilot and Codex, each through its own documented hook, installed with one command or deployed by your device manager. 04. Rules drafted for you, replayed on 30 days. Truehound drafts rules from the calls it has already seen, with Claude on your own Anthropic key or with its built-in rules. Each draft is replayed on the last 30 days of calls so you see what it would have stopped, and nothing applies until an admin approves it. 05. Secrets stripped on the laptop. API keys, tokens, passwords and private keys are replaced with [REDACTED] on the engineer's machine before anything is sent, and the server runs the same check again before it stores a line.

passages.title: AI agent control
passages.heading: And every AI key and agent, with an owner
passages.text: AI key inventory. OpenAI and Anthropic API keys, projects and service accounts, and GitHub Copilot seats, read from each provider's admin API, with the owner and the last use where the provider reports one. Agents and MCP servers. MCP servers and agent tokens on the gateway, sign-ins to AI apps, AI bots and OAuth grants to AI apps, each with an owner. Suspend one, or use the kill switch. Which apps people use. Discovery lists the apps people sign in to, how they got in, what each can reach, and whether it is allowed. Take it back, then prove it. A revoke is checked by a fresh read of the provider. A key still active after the revoke is shown as still present, not as done. The agents Truehound runs for you follow the same rules: see all of them.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.text: Trust Center. How Truehound protects your data, what it has in place today, and what it does not have yet. Every statement is true of the product as it ships. Last updated 2026-10-25. In place. 21. Not yet. 5. SOC 2 report. Not yet. Certifications. None held. Contact. truehoundhq@truehound.io.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Overview
passages.text: This page lists every security and privacy control Truehound has, and every one it does not have yet. “Not yet” means exactly that: we do not have it, and the plan says what we will do. Nothing here is a claim we cannot show you. In place | Partly | Not yet | Sub-processors. 21 | 6 | 5 | 11. On this site, right now. OnAccounts (email sign-in). Signing in keeps your workspace on our servers (Cloudflare D1) for your team. OnApps beyond GitHub, mailbox discovery, browser extension. You can connect other apps, opt in to mailbox metadata discovery and use the extension. CheckingAI features (Anthropic, on your own key). Asking our connector. CheckingDemo-form and report-email capture. Asking our connector. OffProduct analytics (PostHog). No analytics: no page views or clicks leave your browser.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Compliance and reports
passages.text: Not yetCertifications and attestations. Truehound holds no security certification or attestation. No SOC 2 (Type I or Type II), no ISO 27001, no ISO 27701, no HIPAA attestation, no PCI DSS assessment of our own, and no independent penetration test. Our hosting providers publish their own reports for their facilities; those are theirs, not ours. We will not describe Truehound as certified, compliant or audited until an independent party has issued the report. Plan: SOC 2 Type I readiness is the first step, started when a customer needs it. Until then, the questionnaire answers and the evidence on this page are what we can show. Not yetSOC 2 report. Truehound does not have a SOC 2 report. We do not claim one, and will not until an independent auditor issues it. Plan: Start a SOC 2 Type I readiness project when a customer needs it, using the controls on this page as the starting point. Not yetISO 27001. Not held, and not planned before SOC 2. Not yetIndependent penetration test. No third party has tested Truehound yet. Our own checks run on every change (see Application security). Plan: Commission an independent test before accounts hold customer data in production, and share the summary under NDA. In placeData Processing Agreement. GDPR Article 28 terms, US service-provider terms, Standard Contractual Clauses, a security annex and a sub-processor annex, published and ready to sign. In placeSecurity questionnaires.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Compliance and reports
passages.text: A CAIQ-lite style answer pack is published, every answer drawn from how the product works today, with the file that enforces it. We also answer your own questionnaire directly, usually within 5 business days. Email truehoundhq@truehound.io.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Data security
passages.text: In placeData stays in your browser by default. Without an account, tokens, the audit and the workspace are stored in your browser, not on our servers. With an account, your team’s workspace is kept in Cloudflare D1. In placeEncryption in transit. HTTPS everywhere; plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS. The site accepts only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, with forward secrecy (measured with SSL Labs, see Security grades). In placeEncryption at rest. App credentials an admin saves, including one-click app sign-ins, are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived for each workspace (HKDF-SHA256) from a master secret held only in the connector’s secret store; connected-app credentials are bound to their workspace and app, and the master key can be rotated. Sessions, invites, API keys and extension keys are stored only as SHA-256 hashes (sign-in link hashes too, once email sign-in is on). Cloudflare encrypts D1 and Workers KV data at rest. In placeWhat we read, and what we never read. From connected apps: people, accounts, roles, status, dates and grants. Never message, document or email body contents; mailbox discovery is limited to sender, subject and date. Secret values found in code are masked and never kept. PartlyBackups. Cloudflare D1 keeps point-in-time restore for account data automatically (30 days on a paid Workers plan, 7 days otherwise). Demo-form leads in Workers KV have no backup. We have not yet practised a restore. Plan:

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Data security
passages.text: Run and record a restore drill before accounts hold customer data in production. In placeData retention. Retention jobs run every 15 minutes in the connector. Scan history and connected-app scans are kept 90 days (the latest successful scan is always kept); sign-in link records 24 hours; sessions 30 days from your last visit; invites 7 days; review links for outside reviewers 120 days; extension sign-ins 395 days; demo-form leads 24 months. The Proof log is kept for the life of the workspace, because it is the evidence. The full table is in the Privacy Policy. In placeErasure. An owner or admin can export everything a workspace holds as one JSON file; an owner deletes the workspace, and everything stored for it, in one step; a person can delete their account. Retention jobs run every 15 minutes (sign-in records 24 hours, scan histories 90 days, extension sign-ins 13 months, leads 24 months). Restore copies expire within 30 days.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Application security
passages.text: In placeCredential management. Our own secrets (payment, email, GitHub App, encryption) live in Cloudflare’s write-only Worker secrets and GitHub Actions secrets, are pushed by the deploy workflow without being printed, and never reach the browser. Tokens you paste are relayed per request and never stored or logged by our connector. In placeSecure development. TypeScript in strict mode, linting, unit and contract tests, and end-to-end suites. A pre-push gate runs the full validation before code reaches the main branch, the connector deploys only after its own tests run in CI, installs use lockfiles, and GitHub Actions are pinned to exact commits. In placeBrowser hardening. A strict Content Security Policy (scripts only from our own site; connections only to our site, our connector and the apps you connect), a referrer policy, fonts served from our own site and no third-party scripts. In placeOpen hook script. The script that governs AI agents' tool calls runs on your developers' laptops, so you can read every line before you install it: it is published as a plain file at /hooks/truehound-hook.mjs (needs Node 18 or newer). It redacts secrets on the laptop before anything is sent, sends one small request, gives up after 250 milliseconds, and reads its token from a config file with mode 600. PartlyVulnerability and patch management. Dependencies are pinned by lockfile and reviewed by hand when upgraded. Automated dependency alerts are not switched on yet. Plan:

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Application security
passages.text: Switch on GitHub’s dependency alerts and add a dependency audit to CI. In placeResponsible disclosure. A published disclosure policy with safe harbour, a security.txt file, acknowledgement within 1 business day, and fix targets of 14 days for critical and 30 days for high issues.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Access control
passages.text: In placeCustomer data access. Every account query is limited to the workspace it belongs to; a non-member gets “not found”, and automated tests check it. Owner, admin and member roles limit who can change what, and an approval policy can require a second admin. In placeHow Truehound gets access to your apps. You connect with the narrowest read-only sign-in the app offers (for GitHub, a fine-grained read-only token that you create and can revoke; every call is a read). Nothing is changed in an app until a person approves a fix under your approval policy, where the person who proposed a fix can never approve it, and Truehound then reads the app again to verify. AI is optional and runs on your own Anthropic key (bring your own key): Truehound holds no AI key, pays nothing for your AI, and without your key every feature runs on rules and says so. Saved credentials are encrypted per workspace and are never returned to the browser. PartlyProduction access. One person, the founder, can reach production (the Cloudflare, GitHub and Stripe accounts). Nobody else has access. Plan: Confirm and record two-factor sign-in on every production account, and review access each quarter. PartlyLogging. Every change, approval and consent in a workspace is written to the Proof log, a SHA-256 hash chain where tampering shows. The connector keeps no request logs and logs errors without personal data. Plan: Add retained security logging and alerting for the production accounts.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Access control
passages.text: In placePassword security. Truehound has no passwords to steal: you sign in by payment, an activation code, an invite link or a passkey, and connect apps with their own sign-in. Email sign-in links are built but not switched on yet (no email provider is connected), so no sign-in email is sent today. The session cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and limited to our API.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Infrastructure
passages.text: In placeHosting. The website is static files on GitHub Pages, with no server code. The connector and account backend are a Cloudflare Worker, with Cloudflare D1 and Workers KV for storage. We run no servers of our own. In placeData centers. Physical security is GitHub’s and Cloudflare’s. Each publishes its own SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports for its facilities. In placeSeparate production. Production deploys only from the main branch, by CI. Development runs locally on in-memory stores and fixtures, and the public demo uses fictional data only. Customer data is never copied out of production. In placeStatus page. A public status page shows the connector and site health, with samples kept 100 days. It has no incident feed yet, so incident notices go to affected customers by email. It is not an uptime commitment. PartlyBusiness continuity and disaster recovery. The site and connector can be rebuilt and redeployed from source, which is kept in two private repositories. There is no uptime commitment unless an order form gives one. Plan: Write and test a recovery runbook with target times, alongside the restore drill.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Corporate security
passages.text: In placeDevices. Truehound is one person. The founder’s work computer uses full-disk encryption (FileVault, checked 2026-10-22). Not yetSecurity training. There are no employees to train yet. Plan: Security onboarding for every hire before they get any access, and training each year. PartlyIncident response. The process, in order. Report: anyone can report to truehoundhq@truehound.io, and we acknowledge within 1 business day. Triage: we assess severity within 5 business days. Contain and fix: critical issues get a first fix or mitigation within 14 days and high within 30, per the disclosure policy. Notify: we tell affected customers of a personal data breach by email to their account owners within 72 hours of confirming it. Check the service: the status page shows connector and site health. Learn: the disclosure policy and this page are updated when something changes. Not yet done: a rehearsal of this process. Plan: Write the incident runbook and rehearse it once before accounts go live.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Security grades
passages.text: Measured by hand on the date shown, against truehound.io. We publish the grade we got, not the one we want. Check | Grade | Measured | Why | Fix. SSL Labs (Qualys) | B | 2026-10-22 | TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, with forward secrecy, but GitHub Pages still offers two older TLS 1.2 cipher suites (RSA key exchange, CBC) and sends no HSTS header. We cannot change GitHub Pages’ TLS settings. | Put Cloudflare in front of the site (a DNS change) with modern ciphers only and HSTS, which should reach A or A+. Security Headers (securityheaders.com) | F, by its rules | 2026-10-22 | The service blocks automated checks, so we read the response headers ourselves: GitHub Pages sends none of the six it grades (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy). Our Content Security Policy and referrer policy are set inside the page, which browsers enforce but the grader does not count. | The same Cloudflare switch lets us send all six as real headers. SecurityScorecard | Not measured | 2026-10-22 | It needs an account we do not have. | Measure once the Cloudflare switch is done.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Data flow
passages.text: Where your data goes, in the order it moves. How much of this applies depends on whether you use the free scan and browser mode, or an account with the access agent. Data flow: step, what moves, where it goes, and whether it is kept. Step | What moves | Where | Kept? You run a scan in browser mode | A token you paste, and what GitHub or your identity provider returns | From your browser straight to that provider. Some GitHub code searches pass through our connector on Cloudflare for that one request. | The token is used for the request and is not stored by us. The audit stays in your browser. You create an account | Your email, workspace name and role | Our database on Cloudflare (D1). Resend, for account email, is not engaged yet because email is not switched on. | Yes, until you delete the workspace or ask us to. An admin saves a connection for the agent | The app credential, so the agent can watch and act when nobody is present | Our database, encrypted per workspace. | Yes, only when an admin chooses to save it. Removing the connection deletes it. The agent reads and reports | People, accounts, roles and sign-in facts from the apps you connected | Our database, to build the inventory, reviews and the audit trail. | Yes, on the retention schedule in the Privacy Policy. You pay | Billing contact and plan; card details go straight from you to Stripe | Stripe. | Billing records, as the law requires.

passages.title: Trust Center
passages.heading: Data flow
passages.text: You ask the AI rep on our website | The question you type | Cloudflare Workers AI, through our connector. Never Anthropic. | The question (emails and phone numbers masked) and a keyed hash of your IP, for 30 days. You turn on AI features | The facts for one request; never tokens, keys or secret values | Anthropic. | Not kept by Truehound; Anthropic does not train on it. The sub-processors page names every provider, what it can see and where. Get advance notice of changes.

passages.text: Ask for the security overview, policies, DPA or written answers to your questionnaire. To be plain: there is no SOC 2 report and no ISO 27001 certificate to request, because Truehound holds neither today.

passages.title: Sub-processors
passages.heading: Notice of changes, and your right to object
passages.text: Before we add or replace a sub-processor that processes customer personal data, we email every customer’s account owners and billing contact at least 30 days before it starts, and post the change here and in the change feed (Atom; any feed reader can follow it). A customer may object in writing to truehoundhq@truehound.io within that period on reasonable data protection grounds. We will then try to offer a way to use Truehound without that sub-processor; if we cannot, the customer may terminate the affected service and we refund any prepaid fees for the unused period. In an emergency (for example a provider failing), we may replace a sub-processor sooner and will tell customers as soon as we can, with the same right to object. Each sub-processor is bound by written terms at least as protective as our Data Processing Agreement, and we remain responsible to customers for its work.

passages.heading: What is not a sub-processor
passages.text: The apps your admins connect (GitHub, Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra ID, Slack, Okta, your HR, finance, cloud and work tools). Truehound reads them with your own credentials, under your own agreements with those companies. Google Fonts and other font or script networks: our fonts and scripts are served from our own site. Advertising or tracking services: we use none.

passages.heading: Change history
passages.text: Date | Change. 2026-10-26 | Cloudflare Workers AI added for the website's AI rep. The public website has an AI rep, a chat bubble that answers visitors' questions from Truehound's published pages. Its model runs on Cloudflare Workers AI, from Cloudflare, already a sub-processor. It sees only the question a visitor types and passages from our public pages, never customer workspace data. Truehound keeps the question (emails and phone numbers masked) and a keyed hash of the IP address for 30 days. 2026-10-22 | Register checked against the code: Resend, Microsoft, Finch, Merge and Kombo added, each row says when it is engaged. Resend (account email), Microsoft (Teams review messages) and the HR connection services Finch, Merge and Kombo were in use behind switches but missing from the register, and are added. Every row now names the legal entity, the transfer mechanism and when it is engaged. The register is now also public at /subprocessors. 2026-10-20 | Register matches the providers the hosted product actually uses. The register now lists exactly the providers hosted Truehound uses: Stripe (billing), Cloudflare (the connector Worker and Workers KV) and GitHub Pages (hosting), plus PostHog and Anthropic only if those features are enabled. Earlier entries described a hosted architecture and placeholder vendors that Truehound does not use, and are withdrawn. Related documents. Privacy PolicyData Processing AgreementTrust Center.

passages.title: Atlassian access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: What Truehound reads
passages.text: Everyone in your Atlassian organization (Jira, Confluence and the other Atlassian apps): org and site admins, guests, suspended and deactivated accounts, two-step verification for managed accounts, and last activity per app. Not provided by Atlassian. Two-step verification: Atlassian reports it only for accounts your organization manages (verified domain); for other accounts it is not provided. Organizations still on the original user management experience: Atlassian's directory API does not answer for them, so the scan says so instead of guessing. One organization per API key: when the key can manage several organizations, Truehound reads the first one Atlassian lists. One-click suspend needs a single user directory: with several directories, Truehound gives the link and the steps. Bots and app accounts: not listed by Atlassian's user search.

passages.title: AWS IAM access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: Set up
passages.text: 1Make an external ID only you know: run `openssl rand -hex 16` and keep the 32 characters. 2In AWS CloudFormation, create a stack from Truehound's template (truehound-access-audit.cfn.json). Paste the external ID. Leave EnableFixes off to stay read-only. 3When the stack finishes, copy the RoleArn output. 4Fill in the role ARN and the external ID below. Using IAM Identity Center? Create the stack in your management account and fill in its region too. AWS IAM's own guide.

passages.title: Box access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: Set up
passages.text: 1In the Box Developer Console, create a Platform App, choose Server Authentication (Client Credentials Grant). 2In Configuration, set App Access Level to App + Enterprise Access and turn on the Manage users scope. Box has no read-only scope for users, so this one scope reads and also lets Truehound deactivate a user when you confirm. 3In Authorization, submit the app; a Box admin approves it in the Admin Console, Integrations, Platform Apps Manager. 4Copy the Client ID and Client secret (Configuration) and the Enterprise ID (General Settings), and paste them here as clientId:clientSecret:enterpriseId. Our connector trades them for a 60 minute Box token on every request and never stores them. 5Or, to try it once: paste a Developer Token from the Configuration tab. It lasts 60 minutes. Box's own guide.

passages.title: New Relic access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: What Truehound reads
passages.text: Users in every authentication domain, their user type (basic, core, full platform), groups (Admin, User and custom) and last activity. Not provided by New Relic. Two-factor status: not provided by vendor. Removing a user in a SCIM provisioned domain: New Relic refuses it through the API, so remove them in your identity provider. Proof of a removal: the re-read lists every domain's users; in a domain with more than 500 users it cannot prove the user is gone, so the removal is reported as not verified and you check it in New Relic. New Relic EU data center (api.eu.newrelic.com): not read in this version, because our connector reaches api.newrelic.com only. Authentication domains with more than 500 users: only the first 500 of each are read in this version, and the tenant name says so.

passages.heading: What Truehound reads
passages.text: Workspace admins and members, deactivated and unconfirmed members of your Trello Workspace. One Workspace per token: when the token's account is in several Workspaces, Truehound reads the first one Trello lists.

passages.heading: What it can fix
passages.text: Remove a person from Zoom through its API after your approval, then read Zoom again to prove they are gone. Open Zoom's web portal, User Management, Users. Find the person, choose More next to their name, then Deactivate (or Delete, which also returns the license).

passages.title: Zoom access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: Set up
passages.text: 1In the Zoom App Marketplace, choose Develop, Build App, and create a Server-to-Server OAuth app (an account admin or owner must create it). 2Under Scopes, add user:read:list_users:admin and user:read:user:admin to scan. Add role:read:list_roles:admin to show custom role names, and user:update:status:admin to let Truehound deactivate a user when you confirm. 3Activate the app, then copy the Account ID, Client ID and Client secret from App Credentials. 4Fill in the three fields below. Our connector trades them for a one-hour Zoom token on every request and never stores them. Zoom's own guide.

passages.title: Zoom access reviews and offboarding
passages.heading: Plans needed
passages.text: Reading: Any Zoom plan with more than one user (Pro or above), with a Server-to-Server OAuth app an admin creates. Removing: Any Zoom plan with more than one user (Pro or above), with the user:update:status:admin scope. Last sign-in: Any Zoom plan (Zoom's last login time, which it updates at most every three days).

passages.heading: Set up
passages.text: 1Create an OAuth or server-to-server OAuth app in the Zoom App Marketplace with the SCIM2 scope and use its access token. 2Paste the SCIM token here. It stays in this browser and is sent only to the app, through Truehound's relay. Zoom (SCIM)'s own guide.
